answer.worked:
Let the unknown horizontal side of the left triangle be $a$.
$$\begin{align*}a^2&=10^2-8^2\\a^2&=36\\a&=6\\\cot x&=\frac{\mathrm{Adj}}{\mathrm{Opp}}\\\cot x&=\frac68=\frac34\end{align*}$$

Let the unknown hypotenuse of the right triangle be $h$.
$$\begin{align*}h^2&=15^2+8^2\\h^2&=289\\h&=17\\\operatorname{cosec} y&=\frac{\mathrm{Hyp}}{\mathrm{Opp}}\\\operatorname{cosec} y&=\frac{17}{8}\end{align*}$$

Using the horizontal side $6$ found in part a,
$$\begin{align*}\sec x&=\frac{\mathrm{Hyp}}{\mathrm{Adj}}\\\sec x&=\frac{10}{6}=\frac53\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: If $\cos\theta=\frac{2}{7}$, find the possible values of $\sin\theta$ in exact form.

answer.worked:
Use a right-angled reference triangle with adjacent side $2$ and hypotenuse $7$.
$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{Opp}&=\sqrt{7^2-2^2}\\\mathrm{Opp}&=\sqrt{45}\\\mathrm{Opp}&=3\sqrt5\end{align*}$$
Cosine is positive in quadrants I and IV. Sine is positive in quadrant I and negative in quadrant IV.
$$\sin\theta=\pm\frac{3\sqrt5}{7}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: If $\tan\theta=\frac{8}{5}$, find the exact value of $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$ if $\cos\theta<0$.

answer.worked:
Use a right-angled reference triangle with opposite side $8$ and adjacent side $5$.
$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{Hyp}&=\sqrt{8^2+5^2}\\\mathrm{Hyp}&=\sqrt{89}\end{align*}$$
Tangent is positive in quadrants I and III. Since $\cos\theta<0$, $\theta$ lies in quadrant III, where sine and cosecant are negative.
$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta&=-\frac{8}{\sqrt{89}}\\\operatorname{cosec}\theta&=\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\\\operatorname{cosec}\theta&=-\frac{\sqrt{89}}{8}\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
The original equation requires $\cos\theta\ne0$.
$$\begin{align*}(\tan\theta-1)(\sin\theta-\sqrt3\cos\theta)(\sin\theta+\sqrt3\cos\theta)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Consider $\sin\theta-\sqrt3\cos\theta=0$. Divide each term by $\cos\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta-\sqrt3&=0\\\tan\theta&=\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$
Similarly, for the other factor:
$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta+\sqrt3\cos\theta&=0\\\tan\theta+\sqrt3&=0\\\tan\theta&=-\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$
The first factor gives $\tan\theta=1$. Hence
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=1\quad\text{or}\quad\tan\theta=\pm\sqrt3\\\theta&=\frac\pi4,\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}3\qquad(0\leq\theta\leq\pi).\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Prove that $\dfrac{1}{\sin x\cos x}-\cot x=\tan x$.

answer.short: $\dfrac{1}{\sin x\cos x}-\cot x=\dfrac{1-\cos^2x}{\sin x\cos x}=\tan x$, as required.
answer.worked:
For values of $x$ where the expressions are defined,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{1}{\sin x\cos x}-\cot x&=\frac{1}{\sin x\cos x}-\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\\\frac{1}{\sin x\cos x}-\cot x&=\frac{1-\cos^2x}{\sin x\cos x}\\\frac{1}{\sin x\cos x}-\cot x&=\frac{\sin^2x}{\sin x\cos x}\\\frac{1}{\sin x\cos x}-\cot x&=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\\\frac{1}{\sin x\cos x}-\cot x&=\tan x.\end{align*}$$
Thus LHS $=$ RHS.

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Hence solve in the domain $x\in[0,2\pi]$:
$$\frac{\cos^2x-1}{\sin x\cos x}=\sqrt3.$$

answer.worked:
The original denominator requires $\sin x\cos x\ne0$. Using part a,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{\cos^2x-1}{\sin x\cos x}&=-\frac{1-\cos^2x}{\sin x\cos x}\\\frac{\cos^2x-1}{\sin x\cos x}&=-\frac{\sin^2x}{\sin x\cos x}\\\frac{\cos^2x-1}{\sin x\cos x}&=-\tan x.\end{align*}$$
Therefore,
$$\begin{align*}-\tan x&=\sqrt3\\\tan x&=-\sqrt3\\x&=\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{5\pi}{3}.\end{align*}$$
Both values lie in $[0,2\pi]$ and have $\sin x\cos x\ne0$.

entries.description:
Tips for proving identities
• You CANNOT apply operations to both sides when proving statements.
• Convert to sine and cosine: Simplify mixed functions by rewriting everything in terms of sinθ and cosθ.
• Use Pythagorean identities: Replace squared terms using the identities
• Start with the more complex side: It gives more options for simplification.
• Expand brackets: Reveals terms that may cancel or combine.
• Factor expressions: Useful when one side is a product and the other a sum or difference.
• Split fractions: Break up a single fraction into separate terms if the other side has multiple terms.
• Combine fractions: Use a common denominator to merge terms.
• Multiply by the conjugate: For expressions with binomials in the denominator, this can reveal a difference of two squares.
• Simplify both sides: Complex examples will require you to simplify both LHS and RHS separately until they match.
• There can be more than one way to prove an identity. If your solution does not match the provided solutions, it is likely correct if you have followed the rules for proving identities.
